The protagonist looked out the window. There was no doubt. The tree WAS closer to the house than it was yesterday. And why was it decorated with Christmas ornaments? Strange thing for a hot July afternoon. Another deep sip of the whiskey and the thought faded. He wondered what happened to the dog. Was there a dog? He seemed to remember one. Maybe he was just thinking about his companion's old coat. Another sip and the tree became blurry. Ah, the companion. What was her name? Did it matter? She was gone and mostly forgotten. He did remember the gleam in her eye as he fitted the last brick in the cellar wall sealing her in. He smiled. A classic tale of revenge. Didn't they make a movie out of it? Probably. Another sip and the glass was empty. He sighed and went to the kitchen. The large drum of whiskey sat next to the refrigerator like a sullen bank guard. He pumped out enough to fill the tumbler. He kicked the barrel and made a hollow THUMP sound. Almost empty. Good thing he had several full ones in the pantry. He turned back to the living room. He saw an empty dog dish by the door. There WAS a dog! What happened to him? He tried to remember but all that came to mind was his parent glaring at him as he failed yet another attempt to kill a stranger that his parent had brought home for practice. He could still hear the sharp report of the revolver as his parent shot the stranger. He still resented those training sessions. Asking a young boy to kill a grown man seemed highly unreasonable, but Parent was an unreasonable man. He thought about him. Wondering where he was. He'd be about seventy now. Many years and no contact save for a monthly postcard with lyrics written in blood. Parent was still proud of his political party. And Mother. Most people would be aghast if they found their child wearing her new dress, but not Mother. She grabbed his arm and drove him into town and made him go into a department store and buy matching shoes. Ah, Mother. Still sitting behind the wheel of the green car lo these many years. He really should pour gasoline on it and set it on fire or maybe use some of that excess whiskey. He sat in the recliner and realized that the Christmas tree was now in the living room. And the dog was standing on its back legs next to it. The dog was wearing a three piece suit. The tie was knotted immaculately and a handkerchief was folded neatly in the jacket pocket. The dog said something, but he didn't speak that language so the dog used semaphore flags. The message was clear. The tree was an ambassador from a place both very close yet quite far away. He was to finish his drink and accompany it. He closed his eyes and nodded. He hated Tuesdays.

This watch I got here was first purchased by your great-grandfather during a major global conflict. It was bought in a little general store in a southern city. Made by the first company to ever make wrist watches. Up till then people just carried pocket watches. It was bought by a private soldier on the day he set sail for Europe. It was your great-grandfather’s war watch and he wore it every day he was in that war. When he had done his duty, he went home to your great-grandmother, took the watch off, put it an old coffee can, and in that can it stayed until your granddad was called upon by his country to go overseas and fight once again. This time they called it a later global war. Your great-grandfather gave this watch to your granddad for good luck. Unfortunately, your granddad’s luck wasn’t as good as his old man’s. He was a soldier and he was killed, along with the other soldiers at a battle in the Pacific. Your granddad was facing death, he knew it. None of those boys had any illusions about ever leaving that island alive. So three days before the enemy took the island, your granddad asked a gunner on a transport, a man he had never met before in his life, to deliver to his infant son, who he’d never seen in the flesh, his gold watch. Three days later, your granddad was dead. But the gunner kept his word. After the war was over, he paid a visit to your grandmother, delivering to your infant father, his dad’s gold watch.     This watch. This watch was on your daddy’s wrist when he was shot down over a foreign city. He was captured, put in a prison camp. He knew if the enemy ever saw the watch it’d be confiscated, taken away. The way your dad looked at it, that watch was your birthright. He’d be damned if any enemy soldiers were gonna put their hands on his boy’s birthright. So he hid it in the one place he knew he could hide something. His ass. Five long years, he wore this watch up his ass. Then he died of dysentery, he gave me the watch. I hid this uncomfortable hunk of metal up my ass two years. Then, after seven years, I was sent home to my family. And now, little man, I give the watch to you.
